answers.literal_question: For a three-player standard game, how are aliens selected, which flares enter the cosmic deck, how many cards does each player receive, and how is the first player selected?
clauses: Alien selection and reveal timing.
Flares added to the cosmic deck.
Starting hand size.
First-player selection and turn direction.

answer.result: In a three-player game, each player receives two flares and matching sheets, privately chooses one alien, and returns the unused sheet. After every player has chosen and returned unused sheets, reveal all chosen sheets simultaneously before preparing the cosmic deck or dealing starting hands. This is expressly attributed to a later FFG clarification.
Add both flares dealt to each player, including the rejected alien’s flare; add random flares if needed to reach ten total, then shuffle.
Deal eight cards to each player.
Draw destiny until a player color appears; that player starts. Shuffle that card back into the destiny deck. Turns then pass left.

answers.literal_question: What counts as one colony, can several players have colonies on one planet, and do five foreign colonies have to be in different systems?
clauses: Definition of one colony.
Whether multiple players may have colonies on one planet.
Whether the five foreign colonies must be in different systems.

answer.result: A colony is one or more ships of one color on one planet; extra ships of that color there do not create additional colonies.
Yes. Several colors can coexist on one planet, with each color having its own colony.
No. Five foreign colonies may all be in one other system.

answers.literal_question: At the start of an encounter, must the offense retrieve a warp ship if available, and where does the original rulebook place it when the offense has colonies or has none?
clauses: Whether Regroup retrieval is required when a warp ship is available.
Placement when offense has colonies.
Placement under the original rulebook when offense has none.

answer.result: Yes. Offense must retrieve one of its warp ships if available.
Place it on any existing home or foreign colony.

The original rulebook places it directly in the gate when offense has no colonies. The summary separately notes an FAQ exception for a player with no colonies or ships on their turn: that player may instead place it on any home planet.

answers.literal_question: What happens when destiny has only one card left, and what choices does drawing your own color offer if your home system contains a foreign colony or a completely empty planet?
clauses: Procedure when only one destiny card remains.
Choice after drawing own color when a foreign colony is in the offense’s home system.
Choice to reclaim a completely empty home planet and its result.

answer.result: Do not draw the last card. Shuffle it together with the destiny discard pile, then draw from the new deck.
The offense may redraw, or target one chosen foreign colony in its own home system; that colony’s owner is the defense and other colonies there are bystanders.

The offense may instead target a home planet with no ships of any color and move up to four of its ships from any other existing home or foreign colonies onto it. It is reclaimed automatically; this counts as a win and successful encounter, proceeds only through Launch, and can qualify for a second encounter.

answers.literal_question: Without a special power, may offense attack Blue’s foreign colony in Red’s home system after drawing Blue, and who defends Red’s empty home planet if foreign bystanders are present?
clauses: Whether drawing Blue permits attacking Blue’s foreign colony in Red’s home system without a special power.
Who defends Red’s empty home planet and how foreign bystanders are treated.

answer.result: No. Ordinarily a color destiny targets that player in their own home system; the summary says a player cannot attack a foreign colony in a third player’s system absent a special power.
The owner of the home system (Red) defends its home planet even with zero ships there. Other colors’ colonies are bystanders: they add nothing to defense and are not harmed by the encounter.

answers.literal_question: From where and how many ships may the offense launch, may it strip a colony, and can the defense move ships onto or off the targeted planet during Launch?
clauses: Eligible source and number of offense ships.
Whether the offense may strip a colony.
Whether defense can add or subtract target ships during Launch.

answer.result: The offense places one to four ships on the wide end of the gate, drawn from any combination of its existing home and foreign colonies.
Yes. Removing the final ship immediately eliminates that colony; returning ships cannot treat that now-empty location as an existing colony.
No. Defense cannot add or subtract ships on the target during Launch.

answers.literal_question: In what order are allies invited and committed, can someone invited by both sides join both, and where do defensive allies put their ships?
clauses: Invitation and commitment order.
Whether a player invited by both sides can join both.
Placement of defensive allies’ ships.

answer.result: Offense names allies first, then defense invites (possibly the same players). Starting with the player left of offense and proceeding clockwise, each other player accepts one invitation or declines all, then commits ships before the next decides. Neither main player may invite the other.
No. An ally may join only one side or neither; normally an invitation is required.
Each ally contributes one to four ships from any of their colonies. Defensive allies place their ships beside the target planet, not on it.

answers.literal_question: An attacking side has an attack 10 and six ships; defense has attack 12 and four ships. Who wins, and what happens to offense, offensive allies, defense, defensive allies and bystanders?
clauses: Calculate totals and determine the winner.
Disposition of offense, offensive allies, defense, defensive allies, and bystanders after the defense wins.

answer.result: Offense totals 10 + 6 = 16. Defense totals 12 + 4 = 16. Defense wins ties.

Offense and offensive allies go to the warp. Defending and bystander colonies stay. Defensive allies return their committed ships to any existing colonies of their own, which can be different from their ships’ origins; helping defend does not grant them a colony on the defended planet.

answers.literal_question: When offense wins an attack, where do ships on each side go, do existing bystander colonies survive, and does reinforcing an existing colony earn another colony?
clauses: Destination of each side’s ships when offense wins.
Fate of bystander colonies.
Whether reinforcing an existing colony earns another colony.

answer.result: All offense and offensive ally ships land on the target, establishing or reinforcing each color’s colony. Defense and defensive ally ships go to the warp.
Bystanders survive.
No. The colony marker advances only for a newly established foreign colony, not for reinforcing an existing colony.

answers.literal_question: A defensive ally contributes three ships to a winning defense. May they combine cards and warp retrieval as rewards, and where do the allied and retrieved ships go?
clauses: Whether the defensive ally may combine cards and warp retrieval as rewards.
Number/type of rewards and ship destinations.

answer.result: Yes. For each contributed ship the ally chooses either one cosmic-deck card or one own ship retrieved from the warp; the choices can be mixed freely, but the ordinary rule does not allow declining rewards. Declare the full mix before taking any rewards, without inspecting an initial draw first.

Three contributed ships yield three total rewards in any mix of those two kinds. The ally’s committed ships return to any of its existing colonies; each retrieved warp ship may be placed on any of its own colonies.

answers.literal_question: If a main player’s negotiate loses to attack and that player loses three ships to warp while two allied ships also go there, how much compensation is collected, from where, and what if opponent holds fewer cards?
clauses: Which ships count toward compensation and how many cards are collected.
Source of compensation and rule when the opponent has fewer cards.

answer.result: The losing main player gets one compensation card for each of their own ships actually lost to the warp. Here that is three cards; the two allied ships do not count.
Take the cards from the opponent’s hand, randomly without seeing faces (the backs may be seen). If the opponent has fewer than three cards, take their entire hand.

answers.literal_question: When both reveal negotiate, what happens to allies, what may the main players exchange, where may a new colony be granted, what makes a valid deal, and what is the failure penalty/time limit?
clauses: What happens to allies.
What the main players may exchange and where a colony may be granted.
What makes a deal valid and how long the players have.
Failure penalty and second-encounter consequence.

answer.result: Both sides’ allies return their committed ships to their own colonies and cannot participate in the deal.

The main players may transfer cards from their hands and/or each grant the other one colony on a planet where the giver already has a colony, including a foreign colony. The recipient may use any own ships not in the warp; existing ships coexist and the giver need not vacate.

They have one minute. At least one card or colony must actually transfer; the deal may be one-sided, and agreeing to do nothing is invalid. Future promises are unenforceable; agreed card terms must be truthful and honored.
If time expires without agreement, each main player loses three ships of their choice to the warp, and offense cannot take an ordinary second encounter.

answers.literal_question: What does Morph copy and when, does it track later changes to the opponent’s card, and what happens after the encounter?
clauses: What Morph copies and when.
Whether later opponent-card changes carry over.
What happens to Morph after resolution.

answer.result: Morph copies the opponent’s initially revealed encounter card: it copies an attack’s initial value or becomes negotiate if that is what the opponent revealed.
No. Later modifications to the opponent’s card do not automatically carry over; Morph may be modified separately.
After resolution Morph returns to its normal identity and is normally discarded with the other revealed encounter card, unless an effect changes its destination.

answers.literal_question: Who may play reinforcements, when, on which side, and when is the reinforcement response window finished?
clauses: Eligible players and timing for reinforcement play.
Which side it affects and how the response window ends.
Qualification when the revealed card is negotiate.

answer.result: During Reveal, after encounter cards are revealed, either main player or any ally may play reinforcements.

A reinforcement adds its printed amount to either side’s total, even the opposing side. Players may continue responding with reinforcements until all pass; then resolve with the new totals. Bystanders cannot play merely because they are present.

The summary records an official FAQ wording conflict: p3 permits involved players to play on either side regardless of revealed card types, while p4 answers “No” to playing one on a negotiate. It does not resolve that disputed non-attack case, so no definitive ruling for a negotiate pairing is supported.

answers.literal_question: What are the ordinary per-player and per-card flare limits, when does a played flare return to hand, and when does an alien use its own Wild instead of Super?
clauses: Ordinary player flare limit.
Per-flare limit when ownership changes.
When the flare returns.
When an alien uses its own Wild instead of Super.

answer.result: A player may play at most one flare per encounter. A Card Zap targeting the flare also counts against that player limit.
Each flare can be used only once per encounter, even if it changes hands.
Return it to hand immediately after its effect finishes unless its effect says otherwise.
Normally use Wild; if it is your own alien’s flare and your power is available, you must use Super. If your power is lost or zapped, only Wild is available.

answers.literal_question: When offense lacks encounter cards at start of turn, when defense lacks them at Planning, and when offense loses its last one later, what are the hand replacement and ship-return rules? Is playing other cards before replacement compulsory?
clauses: Offense hand replacement at the start of turn and whether other cards must be played first.
Defense hand replacement at Planning.
What happens when offense runs out later.
Where committed ships return.

answer.result: Start Turn occurs only before the first encounter. If offense has no encounter cards, it reveals and discards the remaining hand and draws eight new cards. It may first play legally playable non-encounter cards, but is not required to.
At Planning, a defense with no encounter card reveals/discards its remaining hand and draws eight, repeating until it has an encounter card.
If offense later runs out when it needs to play an encounter card, its turn ends instead of drawing a replacement.
Offense returns its committed ships to its own colonies; each ally returns its committed ships to its own colonies. The normal no-colony relocation rule applies.

answers.literal_question: After a successful first encounter may offense start a second with no encounter card, hoping to obtain one later? What ends an ordinary turn after first or second encounter?
clauses: Whether offense may start a second encounter without an encounter card in hand.
What ordinarily ends a turn after the first or second encounter.

answer.result: No. A second encounter requires at least one encounter card already in offense’s hand; offense cannot start it hoping to draw one before Planning.

A turn normally has one encounter and optionally a second after a successful first. After the second encounter, or an unsuccessful first encounter, the turn passes left. Machine provides an exception.

answers.literal_question: Exactly when is an ordinary alien power lost and regained for home colony count, can it be used one last time upon loss, and does a Cosmic Zap stop every printed part of the sheet?
clauses: When an ordinary alien power is lost and restored, and whether it may be used once more as it is lost.
What Cosmic Zap cancels and whether every sheet clause stops.

answer.result: With fewer than three home colonies, turn the sheet facedown immediately and lose the power; it cannot be used one last time. Turn it faceup again when the player occupies at least three home planets.

Cosmic Zap cancels a power use identified by the sheet’s bold-italic “use” and prevents further uses until the encounter ends. Printed clauses that do not require a power use are not themselves zappable and are not disabled by zapping a use.

answers.literal_question: When contradictory effects really occur simultaneously, what player order resolves them? Can a player generally interrupt a resolving effect with another non-Zap action, and may a power be preemptively Cosmic Zapped?
clauses: Order for genuinely simultaneous contradictory effects.
Whether another action may interrupt a resolving effect.
When Cosmic Zap may be used.

answer.result: Resolve in this order: offense, defense, then other players clockwise starting left of offense.

No general interruption: finish one effect before another, except a Zap or an effect expressly allowing interruption. Once an effect targeting a hand starts resolving, only a Zap or specific interrupt can intervene.
A power may be zapped only when it is being used, not preemptively.

answers.literal_question: When are ordinary five-foreign-colony victories checked, can wins be shared, and what happens when Tick-Tock removes its last token because two main players make a deal that gives both their fifth foreign colony?
clauses: Timing of an ordinary five-foreign-colony victory and whether multiple players can share it.
Tick-Tock setup, token-removing events, and its final-token result.
Outcome when a deal gives two main players their fifth foreign colony as Tick-Tock loses its last token.

answer.result: Check ordinary victory at the very end of Resolution. A player with five current foreign colonies wins; multiple players meeting the condition together share victory.

Tick-Tock starts with ten tokens. Remove one whenever any player wins as defense or any two players make a successful deal. When its last token is removed, Tick-Tock immediately wins; it may also win normally.
All three players share victory: the two deal participants gain their fifth foreign colony and Tick-Tock removes its last token.

answers.literal_question: For Amoeba, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain what ship presence is required to Ooze, when relative to card selection/reveal does it happen, from/to where and how many ships may move, and can a shipless winner receive a colony?
clauses: Eligible role, optionality and phase.
Ship presence and timing for Ooze.
How many and from/to where may ships move.
Whether a shipless winner receives a colony.

answer.result: Ooze is for a main player only; it is optional and occurs in Planning.
After encounter cards are selected but before reveal, the player must have at least one ship in the encounter to use it.

The player may increase or decrease its encounter ships by removing any number (including all) to its colonies or adding any number from any of its colonies; the summary explicitly allows exceeding the normal four-ship maximum.
No. If the player wins with no ships left in the encounter, they cannot receive a colony.

answers.literal_question: For Anti-Matter, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain which card pairing triggers Negation, which side wins, how are own, opposing main-player and both sides' allied ships counted, and which ordinary tie rule remains?
clauses: Eligible role, optionality and phase.
Card pairing and result of Negation.
Treatment of own/opposing main-player ships and allies.
Ordinary tie rule.

answer.result: Negation is for a main player only, mandatory, during Reveal.
After both main players reveal attack cards, use the power to make the lower total win.

The Anti-Matter player’s own encounter ships are subtracted from that player’s attack card. Offensive and defensive allies’ ships are subtracted from their respective side’s attack card. The opposing main player’s ships are counted in the opponent’s otherwise normally calculated total.
Defense still wins ties.

answers.literal_question: For Barbarian, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain which result triggers Loot and Pillage, when relative to compensation, who sees/chooses how many cards, and what happens to the remaining hand?
clauses: Eligible role, optionality and phase.
Trigger and timing relative to compensation.
Who may see/select how many cards and the remainder.

answer.result: Loot and Pillage is offense-only, mandatory, in Resolution.
It triggers after offense wins an encounter, before any compensation is collected.
Barbarian looks at the opponent’s hand and may choose one card for each of its own ships in the encounter, adding those cards to its hand. Then discard the opponent’s remaining hand.

answers.literal_question: For Calculator, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain when is equalizing announced, which revealed card pairing permits it, what changes and what stays fixed, and what values result from attacks15 and8?
clauses: Eligible role, optionality and phase.
When and which pairing permits equalizing.
What changes and what remains unchanged; calculate the requested example.

answer.result: Equalize is for a main player only, optional, in Planning.
After cards are selected but before reveal, it may be declared; it applies if both revealed cards are attacks.
Subtract the lower attack value from the higher, leaving the lower unchanged: 15 versus 8 becomes 7 versus 8.

answers.literal_question: For Chosen, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain how often and when may Divine Intervention be used, how many cards are drawn, what happens with no encounters, what replacements/addition are allowed, and where do replaced/unused cards go?
clauses: Eligible role, optionality, phase and use frequency/timing.
Number drawn and outcome if none are encounters.
Replacement/addition choices and discard destinations.

answer.result: Divine Intervention is for a main player only, optional, during Reveal, once per encounter, after encounter cards are revealed.
Draw three cards. If none are encounter cards, discard all three and there is no further effect.

If any are encounter cards, Chosen may select one to replace its revealed encounter card and discard the replaced card. If both the revealed card and chosen replacement are attacks, Chosen may instead add the chosen attack value to its revealed attack, or replace as normal. Discard all other drawn cards.

answers.literal_question: For Citadel, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain when, where and from what may citadels be placed; which portion requires power use; when/how many activate; what bonus applies; and what happens to activated/unactivated citadels after defense wins or loses?
clauses: Eligible role, optionality and phase.
Placement timing, location and card source.
Which action requires power use and which/how many citadels activate.
Bonus and retention/discard outcomes.

answer.result: Fortification is available to any player, optional, in Planning.
During each player’s turn after destiny is drawn, a player may place an attack card from hand faceup beside any planet in any system as a citadel.

Placement requires no power use. If the planet with one or more citadels is attacked, after encounter cards are selected but before reveal, the player may use its power to activate all citadels on that planet.
Add their combined values to the defense total. If activated and defense loses, discard them. If defense wins or they were not activated, they remain.

answers.literal_question: For Clone, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain when relative to outcome, compensation and discard may Replicate act, and which card does it return to where?
clauses: Eligible role, optionality and phase.
Timing relative to resolution, compensation and discard; card returned and destination.

answer.result: Replicate is for a main player only, optional, in Resolution.
After the encounter is resolved and any compensation is claimed, Clone may return its own encounter card to its hand instead of discarding it.

answers.literal_question: For Cudgel, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain what result and revealed card trigger Smash, how many extra ships must which player lose, who chooses them, and are normal losses replaced? Does successfully making a deal count as a successful encounter, as a win for Cudgel or Barbarian, or both? Cudgel originally reveals a negotiate and then uses Human Wild to turn it into attack 42. Does that transformation satisfy Cudgel's requirement to have revealed an attack?
clauses: Eligible role, optionality and phase.
Trigger and extra loss quantity/selector; relation to normal losses.
Deal success versus win-only effects.
Effect of conversion after revealing negotiate.

answer.result: Smash is for a main player only, mandatory, in Resolution.

It triggers when Cudgel wins an encounter in which it revealed an attack. The opponent must lose extra ships equal to Cudgel’s own ships in the encounter, and the opponent chooses them; this is in addition to normal losses.
A successfully made deal is a successful encounter, but it is not a win for Cudgel or Barbarian.
No. If Cudgel revealed negotiate and Human Wild later converts it to attack 42, it did not reveal an attack, so Smash is not triggered.

answers.literal_question: For Dictator, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain on whose turns and when is Command used, what selection information and choice does it give, and how is destiny handled on Dictator's turn or when zapped?
clauses: Eligible role, optionality and phase.
When and on whose turns Command is used, information and choice.
Destiny procedure on own turn or when zapped.

answer.result: Command is mandatory for a player who is not offense, during Destiny.
Before destiny is chosen, Dictator takes the destiny deck, looks through it, and chooses any card, which is played as though offense drew it.
On Dictator’s own turn, or whenever Dictator is zapped, shuffle the remaining destiny cards and deal one at random.

answers.literal_question: For Fido, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain when may Fetch act, which card is offered to whom, what happens on refusal versus acceptance, and what benefit may Fido receive?
clauses: Eligible role, optionality and phase.
Timing and card retrieved/offered.
Outcomes on refusal or acceptance and benefit to Fido.

answer.result: Fetch is available to any player, optional, in Resolution.
After encounter cards are discarded at the end of the encounter, Fido may retrieve one of those discarded cards and offer it to another player.
If refused, Fido may keep the card. If accepted, the other player keeps it, then Fido may either retrieve one of its ships from the warp or draw one card from the deck.

answers.literal_question: For Filch, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain when may Theft act, whose encounter card is taken from where and added to whose hand?
clauses: Eligible role, optionality and phase.
Timing and card source/destination.

answer.result: Theft is for a main player only, optional, during Resolution.
After encounter cards are discarded at the end of the encounter, Filch may take the opponent’s encounter card from the discard pile and add it to its hand.

answers.literal_question: For Fodder, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain what pairing and timing permit Overwhelm, which hand attack values qualify relative to both revealed attacks, how many can be discarded, and how do they affect the total?
clauses: Eligible role, optionality and phase.
Pairing and timing that permit Overwhelm.
Which hand attacks qualify and how many may be selected.
How the cards affect the total.

answer.result: Overwhelm is for a main player only, optional, during Reveal.
It is permitted after both main players reveal attack cards.
Discard any or all attack cards from hand that are both higher than your own played attack and lower than the opponent’s played attack. Choose all cards for one use together.
Add the values of the discarded cards to your own total.

answers.literal_question: For Gambler, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain when does Bluff act relative to the opponent's reveal, what is announced, what happens if unchallenged, and on challenge who loses how many ships from which locations and how is the encounter then resolved? State the printed incompatible alien.
clauses: Eligible role, optionality and phase.
When Bluff occurs and what is announced; unchallenged result.
What happens upon a challenge if the claim was false or true, including ship count/location and next resolution.
Printed incompatible alien.

answer.result: Bluff is for a main player only, optional, during Reveal.

After the opponent reveals, Gambler may keep its own card facedown and state what the card is; it may lie. If unchallenged, resolve as though its statement were true and place the facedown card on the bottom of the deck instead of discarding it.

If challenged, reveal the card. If Gambler lied, it loses ships equal to its own ships in the encounter; if truthful, the opponent loses ships equal to its ships in the encounter. Those penalty ships cannot be ships involved in the encounter; they are chosen under the losing player’s control from outside the encounter. Then resolve normally using the revealed cards.
The printed restriction is “Do not use with Sorcerer.”

answers.literal_question: For Grudge, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain when are tokens assigned, to whom, what happens for each of Grudge's win/deal and loss/failed-deal branches, who chooses penalty ships and which ships are ineligible?
clauses: Eligible role, optionality and phase.
When tokens are assigned and to whom.
Win/deal and loss/failed-deal branches, ship choices and ineligible ships.

answer.result: Revenge is for a main player only, mandatory, during Alliance.

After alliances form, give a grudge token to each player you invited who did not ally with you. An ally who initially committed at least one ship to you avoids the token even if those ships later leave.

If you win or make a deal, each token holder discards the token and loses one ship of their choice to the warp. If you lose or fail a deal, each token holder discards it and loses four ships of their choice. Ships used to ally with the other side are ineligible. If the penalty calls for outside-encounter ships and none are eligible, lose none.

answers.literal_question: For Hacker, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain when collecting compensation, from whose hand may Hack take cards and who looks/chooses them; when Hacker owes compensation, who selects what the opponent receives?
clauses: Eligible role, optionality and phase.
When collecting compensation, whose hand may be targeted and who inspects/selects.
When Hacker owes compensation, who selects the cards paid.

answer.result: Hack is for a main player only, optional, during Resolution.

When collecting compensation, Hacker may choose which player to collect it from, whether or not that player is the opponent; Hacker looks through that player’s hand and chooses the desired compensation cards.
When an opponent collects compensation from Hacker, Hacker may select the cards the opponent receives.

answers.literal_question: For Hate, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain when does Rage act, what must Hate discard, what alternatives does each other player have, what attack threshold does the original sheet print, who selects lost ships, and what happens if Hate then lacks encounters?
clauses: Eligible role, optionality, phase and timing.
Hate’s discard and the other players’ choices, including attack threshold and who chooses lost ships.
Result if Hate lacks encounter cards after using Rage.

answer.result: Rage is offense-only, mandatory, at Start Turn. At the start of its own turn, Hate first chooses and discards a card from hand. A required new starting hand is drawn before Rage.

Each other player must either discard the same card type or lose three ships of Hate’s choice to the warp. If Hate discarded an attack, other players must discard an attack of equal or higher value (the printed sheet’s threshold); someone with no qualifying attack loses ships instead. A lower attack cannot be discarded to evade the loss.
If Hate has no encounter cards after using Rage, it draws a new hand.

answers.literal_question: For Healer, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain what event and whose losses permit Heal, how many of that event's ships return and where, what card benefit is earned, can several players be healed, and does healing remove compensation?
clauses: Eligible role, optionality and phases.
Event and whose losses permit Heal, quantity/location and card benefit.
Whether several players may be healed and whether healing removes compensation.

answer.result: Heal is available to any player, optional, in Start Turn, Regroup, Destiny, Launch, Alliance, Planning, Reveal, or Resolution.

When another player loses ships to the warp or has ships removed from the game, Healer may return all ships just lost to that player, who places them on any of their colonies; Healer earns one card from the deck.
During an encounter Healer may heal several players, drawing one card for each. Healing happens after warp arrival and does not remove compensation eligibility.

answers.literal_question: For Human, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain when does Humanity act, what bonus does it add to which side, and what happens if this use is zapped?
clauses: Eligible role, optionality and phase.
Timing and bonus applied to which side.
Effect if this use is zapped.

answer.result: Humanity is for a main player or ally, mandatory, during Reveal.
After encounter cards are revealed, add 4 to Human’s own side’s total.
If the power use is zapped, Human’s side automatically wins the encounter, even if either or both players revealed negotiate.

answers.literal_question: For Kamikaze, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain when may Sacrifice act, how many ships from where may be sacrificed, what cards result, and what happens to those ships if the use is zapped?
clauses: Eligible role, optionality and phase.
When, how many and where ships may be sacrificed; card reward.
What happens if the use is zapped.

answer.result: Sacrifice is for a main player only, optional, during Planning.
Before encounter cards are selected, Kamikaze may send up to four of its ships from any of its colonies to the warp. It draws two cards from the deck for each ship sent.
If the power is zapped, the sacrificed ships are not lost to the warp.

answers.literal_question: For Loser, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain when is Upset declared, what card-selection restriction follows, how does it change the outcome and when does that reversal happen relative to other effects including zapped Human?
clauses: Eligible role, optionality and phase.
When upset is declared and card restriction.
How it changes the result and when reversal resolves relative to Human, including zapped Human.

answer.result: Upset is for a main player only, optional, during Planning.
Declare it before encounter cards are selected. Once declared, both main players must play attack cards if possible.
After reveal, reverse the winning and losing sides. This happens after all other game effects have resolved, including Human’s power being zapped; thus a zapped Human win is then reversed by Loser.

answers.literal_question: For Machine, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain after what outcomes may Continuity grant another encounter, how many encounters may its turn contain and what hand requirement remains?

answers.literal_question: For Macron, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain under the retained official erratum, when are Mass's launch/ally limitation and ship-strength uses made, what ship limit applies to offense/allies, how much is each ship worth for total versus compensation/rewards, and does the defense itself have the one-ship launch limit? Each own ship adds 4 to its side’s total; for compensation or rewards, each own ship counts as two ships. The one-ship limit applies to offense or ally, not to the defense.
An effect that asks for a number of ships counts each physical Macron ship as one, not as four.

answers.literal_question: For Masochist, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain when exactly is Hurt Yourself checked, what lost-ship locations count, what is the alternate win condition, is it lost for too few home colonies, and can Masochist still win normally? Mind may not tell any other player what cards it saw using the power.

answers.literal_question: For Mirror, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain when is Reversal declared, which revealed cards are changed, how are digits treated, and what values result from15,20 and08?

answers.literal_question: For Miser, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain what extra hands and choice are given at setup, how may Hoard substitute for the ordinary hand, can gains be put there or opponents inspect/draw from it, and when/how can the hoard be replaced?

If the hoard has no encounter cards, Miser may reveal and discard it, then receive a new eight-card hoard.

answers.literal_question: For Mite, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain when and at what defense hand-size threshold does Bluster act, what two alternatives does defense have, how are cards discarded, and what are ship destinations and encounter status under each choice?

answers.literal_question: For Mutant, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain when and at what hand size may Regenerate act, from which sources and in what sequence/randomness are cards taken, and when does drawing stop?

Draw one card at a time, at random, from any player(s) or the deck until the hand reaches eight.

answers.literal_question: For Observer, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain in what roles may Protect act, whose ships are protected in each role, during what phase and from which loss destination are they returned to where?

answers.literal_question: For Oracle, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain when does Foresee act, whose card is played in what manner first, and when does Oracle then select and play its own?

Only after seeing that card does Oracle select and play its own card.

answers.literal_question: For Pacifist, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain which revealed pairing triggers Peace and who wins, and what happens when both reveal negotiate?

If both reveal negotiate, they attempt a deal as usual.

answers.literal_question: For Parasite, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain when may Infest act, what invitation and side choices does it change, how many ships are sent, and can it override an effect that specifically prevents alliance?

answers.literal_question: For Philanthropist, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain when may Giving act, how many cards from where go to which eligible recipient, when can that card be used, and under what own-hand/role condition is a new hand drawn?

If Philanthropist is a main player and afterwards has no encounter cards in hand, it draws a new hand.

answers.literal_question: For Reincarnator, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain what results trigger Reincarnation, where is the replacement drawn from and which candidates are rejected, what happens on later losses, what old power remains, and under the original printed copying conditional, which powers may another alien copy and what happens when that copier loses?

Losing an encounter or failing a deal triggers it. Draw an alien power at random from the unused pile; redraw if the alien has Game Setup text or is not allowed in the game.

answers.literal_question: For Remora, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain what separate retrieval and draw events permit Cling, how much is obtained per event, where do the benefits come from, and what same-encounter retrieval restriction applies?

Remora may not retrieve a ship in the same encounter in which that ship went to the warp.

answers.literal_question: For Reserve, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain when may Reinforce turn which attack cards into what value, how many may it use, and what cost cancels another player's reinforcement and where does that canceled card go?

When another player plays a reinforcement, Reserve may use its power and discard a negotiate card to cancel it; the canceled reinforcement is discarded.

answers.literal_question: For Shadow, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain which destiny draws trigger Execute, who chooses whose ship from which location, how is wild handled and must its target match offense's chosen defense?

answers.literal_question: For Sorcerer, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain when relative to selection/reveal does Magic act, what is switched, and which card does each player reveal afterward?

Each player then reveals the card received from the opponent.

answers.literal_question: For Spiff, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain under the retained official crash-landing erratum, what card pairing, losing margin and role permit Crash Land, how many ships escape what loss and land where, and which coexistence restrictions remain? The ship coexists with ships already there, except this does not override a place or alien rule that prohibits coexistence.

answers.literal_question: For Tick-Tock, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain how many tokens are set up in the standard five-planet game, which two types of events remove tokens, what happens at the final token, and can Tick-Tock still win normally?

answers.literal_question: For Trader, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain when may Transference act, which hands are exchanged and who keeps which hand afterward?

answers.literal_question: For Tripler, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain when does Thrice act, what card type is required, what happens at values10-or-less versus above10, and what rounding applies? Calculate attacks10 and11.

answers.literal_question: For Vacuum, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain what event triggers Catharsis, how many additional ships may be lost, who chooses targets/quantities versus exact colony sources, can Vacuum target itself, and are these losses additional to ordinary losses?

answers.literal_question: For Virus, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain when does Multiply act, how are its own ships and attack card combined, how are allied ships counted, and what total results from attack8, three own ships and two allied ships?

Starting with six ships and facing three losses, only one can be eradicated while preserving five; the other two go to the warp.

answers.literal_question: For Void, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain what result and role trigger Eradicate, whose ships go to which destination, what minimum number of surviving ships is protected in this standard game and where do excess losses go? answers.literal_question: For Vulch, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain whose discarded artifacts trigger Salvage, does played versus unplayed matter, can it salvage its own played artifacts, and what special reveal/retention/new-draw procedure applies when refreshing a hand?

answers.literal_question: For Will, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain under the official timing correction, when does Choice act, how may it change the opponent/location, what third-player-system colony requirement remains, and do other effects of the drawn destiny card still occur?

answers.literal_question: For Zombie, state the eligible player role, whether use is optional or mandatory, and its phase(s); then explain when does Immortality prevent a warp loss, where are ships sent instead, which additional deal clause does not require power use, who may be liberated under the FAQ and where do freed ships go? answers.literal_question: A player must draw from the cosmic deck, but both it and its discard pile are empty. What procedure makes a new deck and hands? If that still cannot provide full hands, what happens to Miser's hoard and other setup card holdings?

answers.literal_question: Do Zombie ships kept out of the warp by Zombie's power and ships eradicated by Void earn negotiate compensation? Would Zombie instead qualify if its power were zapped and those ships actually reached the warp?

answers.literal_question: For base effects, distinguish ships that are losing an encounter, ships lost to the warp, and ships sent to the warp. Can a losing Zombie ship avoid becoming lost, and do ships sent by a separate effect count as lost?

A Zombie ship can avoid becoming lost to the warp by being prevented from arriving there.

answers.literal_question: Before compensation starts, may you legally play a reinforcement to remove it from your hand? Once Hacker has targeted your hand, may you then dump it, and what kinds of effects can interrupt the hand-targeting action?

answers.literal_question: When Mobius Tubes releases a player's ships and that player has no colonies, where do those ships end up? What extra placement can the offense make before remaining ships return to the warp?

answers.literal_question: Does Start Turn happen on both encounters of a turn or only the first? If the offense needs a new hand and another player wants to use a Regroup Plague, which happens first?

Order between offense hand replacement and another player’s Regroup Plague.

answers.literal_question: When discard order matters, in what order are non-encounter cards discarded, and how are the main players' encounter cards ordered so that one ends on top?

Order for main players’ encounter-card discards and which encounter card ends on top.

answers.literal_question: When offense automatically reclaims a completely empty home planet after drawing its own color, through which encounter phase does play proceed? Number/source of ships that may be moved to reclaim it.

Move up to four offense ships from any of its other existing home or foreign colonies onto that empty planet.

answers.literal_question: If you have no ships outside the encounter, may you pay a Void Wild cost that specifically requires an outside ship using an involved ship? If Grudge instead requires outside ships to be lost when none exist, how many do you lose?

No. Winning alone does not give offense a colony without a ship to land, unless a specific effect allows it.

answers.literal_question: With no effect granting an exception, may a player lie about hand contents, show those cards, conceal how many cards are held, or conduct private table talk?
clauses: Whether hand-content claims may be false.
Whether cards may be shown or hand size concealed.
Whether table talk may be private.

answer.result: Yes. A player may make claims or lie about hand contents during ordinary public table talk; agreed deal terms must still be truthful and honored.
No. Card faces remain private unless an effect permits showing them; hand size is public, so it cannot be concealed.
No. Table talk is public unless an effect permits secrecy.

answers.literal_question: For encounter totals, is a modified card used at its original printed value or its current value? For an effect unrelated to encounter resolution that targets a card's identity, which identity is used, and does Morph cease to be a Morph by identity after copying an attack? Unless a specific effect says otherwise, which type/value do effects strictly determining compensation, rewards or disposition of involved ships use?
clauses: Card value/type for encounter resolution after modification.
Identity used for unrelated effects that target a card.
Whether Morph’s identity changes after copying.
Type/value for effects determining compensation, rewards, or involved-ship disposition.

answer.result: Use the card’s current modified type/value for encounter resolution.
For other effects, normally use the card’s original printed identity.
No. Morph’s printed identity remains Morph after copying an attack.
Use the current modified card type/value for these encounter-resolution effects, unless a specific effect says otherwise.

answers.literal_question: Are discard piles ordinarily public, and may other players inspect every card discarded faceup in a simultaneous group before deciding how to respond?
clauses: Whether discard piles are public.
Whether every card in a simultaneous faceup discard group may be inspected before responding.

answer.result: Yes. Discards are faceup and public.
Yes. Cards discarded together are faceup and public, so players may inspect the full group before deciding how to respond.

answers.literal_question: After losing its alien power, is a player still considered to be that alien for effects that care about alien identity?
clauses: Whether alien identity remains after power loss.

answer.result: No. Losing the power also removes that alien identity for effects that depend on alien identity.

answers.literal_question: Can Fodder or Reserve discard one attack for its power, observe the result, and then add more in another use during that Reveal phase? Can Kamikaze sacrifice and draw one ship at a time to decide how many to sacrifice?
clauses: Whether Fodder/Reserve may use one card, inspect the result, and add more in another use that phase.
Whether Kamikaze may sacrifice and draw one ship at a time to choose the amount.

answer.result: No. Fodder and Reserve must choose all cards for one use together; they cannot inspect a result and then make another use to add more.
No. Kamikaze must choose and sacrifice all ships for the use together before drawing cards.

answers.literal_question: Although defensive allies physically place ships next to the target planet, are those ships considered in the hyperspace gate for effects using that phrase?
clauses: Physical placement of defensive allies’ ships.
Whether those ships count as in the gate for effects referring to the gate.

answer.result: Defensive allies place ships beside the target planet, not on it.
Yes. For effects referring to the hyperspace gate, defensive allies are considered in the gate.

answers.literal_question: Unless an effect says otherwise, who chooses which ships a player loses as an extra penalty, and must a chosen ship be under that player's control?
clauses: Who chooses extra penalty losses by default.
Whether chosen ships must be under the player’s control.

answer.result: Unless the effect specifies otherwise, the losing player chooses which ships to lose.
Yes. Forced losses normally choose ships the player controls, not ships already in the warp, removed from the game, or captured.

answers.literal_question: When Plague requires one card of each type held, which types exist in the original base cosmic deck? Is Morph a separate type, and is encounter an additional type?
clauses: Original base card types for a “one of each type” requirement.
Whether Morph and encounter are separate card types.

answer.result: The six base card types are attack, negotiate, Morph, reinforcement, flare, and artifact.
Morph is a distinct card type. “Encounter” is a category, not another card type.

answers.literal_question: If chosen aliens conflict because one has a printed Do Not Use restriction, which alien leaves the game? What two replacement options does the affected player have, and what happens if another conflict is drawn?
clauses: Which alien is removed when a printed Do Not Use restriction creates a conflict.
Two replacement options for the affected player.
What happens if another conflict is drawn.

answer.result: Remove the alien bearing the printed restriction; keep the unrestricted alien.
The affected player may take their originally rejected alien, or draw a replacement unused flare and take that alien.
Redraw replacements that create another conflict until the selection is allowed.

answers.literal_question: Is an encounter legal if gaining a foreign colony would necessarily require making a deal, rather than being possible without a deal?
clauses: Whether an encounter requiring a deal to gain a foreign colony is legal.

answer.result: No. A legal encounter must be one where offense can ultimately gain a foreign colony without having to make a deal.

answers.literal_question: Are alien powers universally limited to one use per encounter? What usage rule applies absent specific text, and how do Hate and Vulch illustrate explicit/context-based limits?
clauses: Whether all alien powers have a universal one-use-per-encounter limit.
General use rule absent specific text.
How Hate and Vulch illustrate context-based limits.

answer.result: No. There is no universal one-use-per-encounter rule.
Absent a specific limit, powers are normally usable once per relevant context.
Hate’s Rage is tied to the start of its own turn; Vulch’s Salvage triggers whenever another player discards an artifact, so its explicit triggering context governs repeated eligible events.

answers.literal_question: If another player's timely action or the timing-order result changes the state after you announce an optional power/effect, may you change your mind about invoking it?
clauses: Whether the owner of an optional effect may reconsider after another action/timing order changes the state.

answer.result: Yes. An optional effect’s owner may change their mind when another effect or the timing order changes the game state.

answers.literal_question: When granting a deal colony, must you vacate your own colony? Can a valid deal be one-sided? Can future promises be added and enforced, and may a player lie about explicit card terms in the agreed deal?
clauses: Whether the giver must vacate a colony granted in a deal.
Whether a one-sided deal can be valid.
Whether future promises can be added/enforced and whether explicit card terms may be false.

answer.result: No. The giver may keep its ships there; existing ships coexist, and vacating would eliminate the colony being offered.
Yes. A deal may be one-sided, but at least one card or colony must actually transfer.
Future promises are unenforceable. Deal terms about cards must be truthful and honored; a player may not lie about explicit agreed card terms.

answers.literal_question: If a flare itself is Card Zapped, does the attempted play use that player's one-flare allowance? Compare a flare prevented by Anti-Matter: does it stay in hand, use the allowance, or become available to attempt again later that encounter?
clauses: Whether Card Zap of a flare consumes the player’s flare allowance.
Compare Anti-Matter prevention: hand destination, allowance, and whether it may be retried.

answer.result: Yes. A Card Zap targeting the flare counts against that player’s one-flare-per-encounter limit.
If Anti-Matter prevents the flare before play, it stays in hand and does not use the flare allowance, but it cannot be attempted again that encounter.

answers.literal_question: Your power is zapped, so you use your own alien's Wild flare. Its text would normally give the flare to that alien or discard it if that alien is absent. Do you keep it, give it away, or discard it after resolution?
clauses: Destination of a player’s own Wild flare after its effect.

answer.result: Keep it after resolution; when your own Wild would otherwise be handed to your alien, the flare rules say to keep it.

answers.literal_question: If a Super flare lets an alien use its power as an ally or in a phase outside the sheet's ordinary highlighted phases, can the actual power use still be Cosmic Zapped in either case?
clauses: Whether a Super-enabled power use may be zapped outside its ordinary role/phase.

answer.result: Yes. If a Super flare enables a power use, that actual use can still be Cosmic Zapped even when the use is outside the sheet’s ordinary role or phase.

answers.literal_question: A player has already played its Super flare, and the power use enabled by it is Cosmic Zapped. Must the flare be discarded or its Wild used immediately? While the power is zapped, which effect would apply to a legal flare play, and does the zap permit that already-played flare to be played a second time in the same encounter?
clauses: What happens to the played Super flare when its enabled power use is zapped.
Which effect applies to a later legal flare play while power is zapped.
Whether the already-played flare may be replayed in the same encounter.

answer.result: The flare remains in hand after its effect finishes; zapping the power does not undo the flare or force it to Wild or discard.
While the power is zapped, only Wild is available for an otherwise legal flare play.
No. The flare has already been used once this encounter, so the zap does not permit replay; ordinary player and per-flare limits still apply.

answers.literal_question: May you wait to see Chosen's divine-intervention cards or the card Philanthropist gives before deciding to Cosmic Zap that power? If you pass and later reinforcements change the winner, or play moves into the next phase, may you then retroactively Zap that earlier use?
clauses: Whether the Zap decision may wait for Chosen’s draw or Philanthropist’s card.
Whether the decision can be delayed until reinforcements change the result or after the phase.

answer.result: Yes. You may see Chosen’s drawn cards or the card Philanthropist gives, then decide whether to Zap within that same phase’s immediate Zap window.
No. If you pass, you cannot later undo the earlier use after reinforcements change the outcome or once play moves to the next phase.

answers.literal_question: If an alien is Cosmic Zapped during Start Turn, does its power return for Regroup or another later phase of that same encounter?
clauses: Whether a zapped power returns later in the encounter after being zapped at Start Turn.

answer.result: No. Zapping a power cancels it and prevents further uses until the encounter ends, so it does not return for Regroup or a later phase that encounter.

answers.literal_question: Amoeba legally invokes ooze to move all twenty ships, which will reduce its home colonies below the power-maintenance threshold. Does loss of its power interrupt the move, or when does the loss occur?
clauses: Whether power loss interrupts Amoeba’s simultaneous movement.
When the power loss occurs.

answer.result: No. The move is carried out simultaneously; Amoeba may move all twenty ships before losing power due to the resulting loss of home colonies.
The power loss occurs after the move has been completed and the home-colony threshold is recalculated.

answers.literal_question: A player initially joins Grudge with at least one ship, then all its allied ships leave through Amoeba Super or Force Field. Does the player still count as having allied, and does it receive a Grudge token for that encounter?
clauses: Whether the player still counts as having allied after its ships leave.
Whether Grudge assigns it a token.

answer.result: Yes. A player that initially committed at least one ship to Grudge counts as having allied even if all its allied ships later leave through Amoeba Super or Force Field.
No. That player avoids a Grudge token.

answers.literal_question: May Amoeba Wild increase a player's ship count when that player is defending with zero ships?
clauses: Whether Amoeba Wild can increase a defender’s ship count from zero.

answer.result: Yes. Amoeba Wild can increase a defense ship count of zero.

answers.literal_question: After being played once, do Anti-Matter Super, Cudgel Super, Kamikaze Super, Machine Super, Masochist Super, Miser Super, or Machine Wild automatically apply in later encounters, or must the corresponding flare be played again each encounter its effect is desired? For otherwise legal uses, what timing phrases does the official FAQ quote for the effects of Kamikaze Super, Machine Super, Masochist Super, Miser Super and Cudgel Super? For the first three, does the quoted wording refer to every player's Regroup or to the user's own Regroup phases?
clauses: Whether the listed flares apply automatically in later encounters.
When each must be played again if its effect is desired.
Official FAQ timing wording for Kamikaze/Machine/Masochist Super, Miser Super, and Cudgel Super.
Whether the first three clauses refer to all players’ or the user’s Regroup phases.

answer.result: No. A flare’s effect does not carry automatically into later encounters; the flare must be played again in each encounter where its effect is wanted.
That applies to Anti-Matter Super, Cudgel Super, Kamikaze Super, Machine Super, Masochist Super, Miser Super, and Machine Wild. Machine Wild must be played when wanted.
The FAQ wording is: Kamikaze, Machine, and Masochist Super “During each of your own Regroup phases”; Miser Super “At the start of each of your encounters”; Cudgel Super “Whenever you use your power.”
The Regroup phrase is each of the user’s own Regroup phases, not every player’s Regroup.

answers.literal_question: Is Chosen's Super flare played before Chosen looks at its divine-intervention cards, or after inspecting them?
clauses: When Chosen Super is played relative to inspecting intervention cards.

answer.result: Chosen Super is played after inspecting the three divine-intervention cards.

answers.literal_question: What happens to existing citadels when Citadel's sheet is turned facedown through power loss, and what happens if that sheet is discarded?
clauses: What happens to citadels when Citadel’s sheet is turned facedown.
What happens when that sheet is discarded.

answer.result: Existing citadels remain when the sheet is turned facedown.
If the sheet is discarded, the citadels are discarded.

answers.literal_question: After Sorcerer switches the encounter cards, which final card does Clone keep and which does Filch take?
clauses: Which card Clone keeps after Sorcerer switches.
Which card Filch takes.

answer.result: Clone keeps the encounter card that ends up in front of Clone after the switch.
Filch takes the card that ends up in front of its opponent after the switch.

answers.literal_question: If Clone, Filch and Fido all have possible claims on played encounter cards, does Clone keep its card before the others act, and how is priority between Filch and Fido decided?
clauses: Whether Clone keeps its claim before Filch/Fido act.
How priority between Filch and Fido is determined.

answer.result: Yes. Clone’s keep takes precedence; the kept card is not discarded.
Filch and Fido resolve their competing claims using ordinary timing.

answers.literal_question: When Clone Super permits up to double normal compensation, must Clone choose exactly normal or exactly double, or may it choose an intermediate amount? Must the opponent have sufficient cards for the chosen compensation amount?
clauses: Whether Clone Super requires exactly normal or exactly double compensation.
Whether the opponent must have enough cards for the chosen amount.

answer.result: Clone may choose any amount from normal compensation through double; it need not choose exactly one endpoint.
Yes. The opponent must have sufficient cards for the amount Clone chooses.

answers.literal_question: Does Mind's ability to inspect another player's hand also permit inspection of Miser's hoard?
clauses: Whether Mind may inspect Miser’s hoard.

answer.result: No. Miser’s hoard is not a hand that Mind may inspect; other players also may not look at it.

answers.literal_question: Can Fido retrieve encounter cards discarded to Plague, Fodder or Reserve during the encounter, or only the encounter cards actually played as such?
clauses: Whether Fido may take encounter cards discarded to other effects or only cards actually played as encounter cards.

answer.result: Fido may retrieve an encounter card actually played as such, not an encounter card merely discarded by Plague, Fodder, or Reserve.

1.heading: Setup
1.text:
## Setup

1. Put the warp in the center. Each player takes five planets of one color, places four of their twenty ships on each, and places their colony marker beside the warp's 0 space.
2. Remove destiny cards naming unused player colors; shuffle the rest, including wilds and specials.
3. Shuffle the flares, deal two to each player, and give them the matching alien sheets. Each secretly chooses one alien, initially placing it facedown, and returns the other sheet to the box. After all players have made their private choices and returned the unused sheets, reveal all chosen alien sheets simultaneously, before preparing the cosmic deck and dealing starting hands. This timing is an explicitly attributed later publisher clarification: revised FFG rulebook p16, Advanced Setup step4, uses the same two-flare/select-one procedure. The original2008 setup does not state that reveal window; no retroactive erratum or historical intent is claimed. The original50-alien selection remains standard here; Hidden Powers is a separate excluded variant. Green/yellow/red indicate recommended experience, not strength. Beginners may start with green aliens without flares.
4. Add **both flares dealt to every player**, including rejected aliens' flares, to the cosmic deck. Add random extras if needed to reach ten flares total; shuffle. Deal eight-card hands. Keep card faces private unless an effect allows showing them.
5. Draw destiny until a player color appears; that player starts. Shuffle the drawn card back into the destiny deck. Play passes left thereafter.

Apply printed alien Game Setup instructions as well. If chosen aliens have a printed incompatibility, remove the alien bearing the restriction, keeping the unrestricted alien. Its player may use their originally rejected alien or draw a replacement unused flare and take that alien, redrawing conflicts. Gambler's printed restriction is **Do not use with Sorcerer**; using them together is an optional FAQ-permitted relaxation, outside this standard setup.

2.heading: Overview
2.text:
## Overview

This summary covers the original **Fantasy Flight English 2008 CE01** game for 3–5 players, including its fifty original aliens, normal flare system and applicable official FAQ rulings. Optional Technology, Four Planets, Hidden Powers, Rotating Powers and Freewheeling Flares are excluded, as are Anniversary bonus content and all expansions. Read an individual card's printed effect and timing when playing it; the flare rules below explain the shared system rather than reproduce every flare card.

Each player leads an alien trying to establish five **foreign colonies**. A colony is one or more ships of one color on one planet; extra ships on that planet do not make extra colonies. Several colors can coexist there, each with its own colony. Home colonies are in your own system; foreign colonies are outside it. Five foreign planets can all be in one other system. Alien powers override conflicting general rules.

3.heading: 1. Regroup
3.text:
### 1. Regroup

Offense must retrieve one of its ships from the warp if available, placing it on any existing home or foreign colony. The original rulebook puts this retrieved ship directly in the gate if offense has no colonies. The FAQ adds that a player who has no colonies or ships on their turn may instead place the Regroup ship on any home planet. Ordinary relocation with no colony to receive ships sends them to the warp; the stated Regroup exceptions take precedence.

4.heading: 2. Destiny
4.text:
### 2. Destiny

Draw destiny to determine the defense and target system. **When only one card remains, do not draw it**: shuffle it with the destiny discards, then draw from the new deck.

- Another player's color: encounter that player in their home system.
- Your own color: redraw, or target one chosen foreign colony in your home system, making its owner the defense. Other colonies there are bystanders. You can instead aim at a home planet with **no ships of any color**, moving up to four of your ships from any of your other existing home or foreign colonies onto that empty home planet to reclaim it automatically. This counts as a win and successful encounter, proceeds only through Launch, and can qualify you for a second encounter.
- Wild: choose another player and encounter them in their home system.
- Special: follow its conditions, defense and location. The original rulebook's illustrated special card chooses the other player with the most current foreign colonies, excluding offense. Break a tie toward offense's left, choosing the first tied eligible player there; encounter that player in their home system (rulebook p7). For color-dependent effects such as Shadow, treat it as the designated defense's color. If a special card designates you as the defense, the original rulebook also permits trying to drive out a foreign colony in your home system: choose one other player's colony as the defense; all other colonies are unaffected bystanders.

Destiny hazard symbols have no effect in this base game. Ordinarily you cannot attack a player's foreign colony in a third player's system: a color/wild/special targets its defense in that player's home system, while your own color permits driving out a foreign colony in your own system. If you already have colonies on **all planets in the defensive system**, draw destiny again.

5.heading: 3. Launch
5.text:
### 3. Launch

The offense chooses one planet in the destiny-indicated system and aims the gate at it. Place one to four offense ships on the **wide end of the hyperspace gate**, drawn from any combination of the offense's existing home and foreign colonies. You may strip a colony, but removing its last ship immediately eliminates it. Ships returning from an encounter or warp cannot return to that now-empty location as though it remained your colony.

Defense cannot add or subtract ships on the target. The owner of a home system defends their planet even with zero ships there. Other colors' colonies are **bystanders**: they add nothing to the defense and the encounter result does not harm them. When driving out a foreign colony, target only that one color's colony; all other colors are bystanders.

If you cannot put any ship in the gate or the last offensive ship is removed, continue the encounter. Winning alone does not give offense a colony without a ship to land, unless a specific effect allows it.

6.heading: 4. Alliance
6.text:
### 4. Alliance

Offense names invited allies first; they wait to answer. Defense then invites allies, possibly including the same players. Neither main player may invite the other. Starting with the player left of offense and proceeding clockwise, each other player accepts one invitation or declines all, then commits ships before the next player decides. You may join only one side or neither; normally an invitation is required.

Each ally contributes one to four ships from any of their colonies. Offensive allies place them on the gate; defensive allies place them beside the target planet, **not on it**. The FAQ nevertheless considers defensive allies in the gate for effects referring to that location. Parasite changes invitation eligibility.

7.heading: Attack against attack
7.text:
### Attack against attack

Each side's total is its main player's attack value plus all ships on its side: offense and offensive allies in the gate; defense on the target plus defensive allies beside it. Higher total wins; **defense wins ties**. Powers and played cards may change this calculation or the winner.

- **Offense wins:** all offense and offensive ally ships land on the target, establishing or reinforcing each color's colony. Defense and defensive ally ships go to warp. Bystanders survive. Advance a colony marker only for a newly established foreign colony, not reinforcement of an existing colony.
- **Defense wins:** defending and bystander colonies stay. Offense and offensive allies go to warp. Defensive allies return their committed ships to any existing own colonies, even different origins; helping defend does not grant a colony on the defended planet. Each defensive ally must collect **one defender reward per ship contributed**. For each contributed ship, draw one cosmic-deck card or retrieve one own warp ship to any own colony; combine these choices freely. The ordinary rule does not permit declining these rewards. Declare the full mix of card draws and warp-ship retrievals **before taking any rewards**; do not inspect an initial draw before deciding the remaining sources (official FAQ p8's base-relevant reward-source rule).

11.heading: Attack against negotiate: compensation
11.text:
### Attack against negotiate: compensation

The negotiate player automatically loses; resolve the winner's ship destinations normally. The losing main player randomly takes one card from the opponent's hand for each of **their own ships actually lost to the warp**. Exclude allied losses: allies receive no compensation. If the opponent lacks sufficient cards, take the entire hand. Cards are taken without seeing their faces. For random hand-card selection, including compensation, you may see which card backs you select; “at random” means without seeing card faces (FAQ p5). Compensation is stolen hand cards; defender rewards are deck draws and/or warp retrieval.

No compensation for ships prevented from reaching the warp (Zombie/Observer) or removed by Void. Healer returning ships **after** they enter the warp does not remove compensation eligibility. Special winners such as Human/Pacifist can change who wins; compensation still requires the relevant attack-versus-negotiate condition.

12.heading: Negotiate against negotiate: making a deal
12.text:
### Negotiate against negotiate: making a deal

Both sides' allies return ships to their own colonies, gain nothing and cannot participate in the deal. The main players have **one minute**. They may transfer cards from their hands and/or each grant the other **one colony on a planet where the giver already has a colony**, including a foreign colony. The recipient can use any own ships not in the warp. Existing ships coexist; the giver need not vacate, and vacating would eliminate the colony being offered. Return any remaining gate ships to offense's colonies.

A successful deal must actually transfer at least one card or colony; it may be one-sided. You cannot agree to do nothing. Tangible terms are restricted to permitted cards/colonies and specific power/card exceptions such as Zombie's liberation; future promises are unenforceable. Card terms may be explicit or vague but must be truthful and honored (if you promise your highest attack, give it). If time expires without agreement, **each main player loses three ships of their choice to the warp**, and offense cannot take an ordinary second encounter. Successful deals qualify for an ordinary second encounter but do not trigger win-only powers.

13.heading: Morph
13.text:
### Morph

The single base Morph becomes an exact copy of the opponent's initially revealed encounter card: attack copies its initial value, negotiate becomes negotiate. Resolve that pairing normally. Subsequent modifications of the opponent's card do not automatically carry over to Morph; Morph can be modified separately. For example, Tripler revealing Morph against attack12 copies12 and divides its own copy to4; Tripler revealing12 against Morph changes its own12 to4, while opponent's Morph remains12. After resolution, Morph returns to its normal identity and is normally discarded with the other revealed encounter card, unless an effect changes its destination. If two Morphs could be played against each other, both sides would lose all involved ships to warp; there is only one in this base deck.

For encounter resolution (card types/values, totals, winner/loser, deals, compensation/rewards and involved ship disposition), use current modified card type/value. Other effects normally refer to original printed identity. Morph's printed identity remains Morph. A later card conversion does not change what card was originally revealed for a reveal-trigger condition.

14.heading: Artifacts and reinforcements
14.text:
### Artifacts and reinforcements

Artifacts are not encounter cards. Follow each artifact's printed effect, permitted role and timing; normally discard after play. **Any player, including an uninvolved bystander, may play Cosmic Zap** on an otherwise legal power use. It cancels that use, including your own, and prevents further uses for that encounter. Cards that cancel cards follow their own printed instructions.

Reinforcements are not encounter cards. During Reveal, after encounter cards are revealed, either main player and any ally may play them to add the card's **printed amount to either side's total**, including the opposing side. Players may respond with further reinforcements until all pass; then resolve using the new totals. Bystanders cannot play them merely because they are present on the planet.

**Official FAQ wording conflict:** FAQ p3 explicitly permits involved players to play reinforcements on either side regardless of the revealed card types; p4 also answers “Can you play a reinforcement card on a negotiate?” with “No.” The ordinary attack-total procedure above is unambiguous. The supplied FAQ does not explain whether its p4 answer means a reinforcement cannot change the negotiate card itself or contradicts its p3 permission. These statements should be checked against a publisher clarification before ruling on that disputed non-attack case.

15.heading: Flare system
15.text:
### Flare system

Flares are not encounter cards. Each has printed Wild and Super effects, usage roles and timing. Normally use Wild; if it is your own alien's flare and your power is available, **you must use Super**, not choose Wild. If your power is lost or zapped, you can use only Wild until your power returns.

Return a flare to hand **immediately after its effect finishes**, rather than discard it, unless its effect states otherwise. A player may play **at most one flare per encounter**, and an individual flare can be used **only once per encounter even if it changes hands**. A Card Zap targeting the flare counts against the player's limit. Prevention of play differs from cancellation after play: see Anti-Matter's FAQ exception. If a Super enables a power use, that power can still be Cosmic Zapped even outside its usual role/phase. The flare remains in hand rather than being discarded or forced to Wild; Only Wild is available for an otherwise legal play while the power is zapped.
